extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims are directed to judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) and whether additional claim elements integrate the exception into a practical application or add an inventive concept under Step 2A/2B of the Alice/Mayo framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more than the exception (Step 2B), examiners should ask whether the additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) or are more than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The additional element(s) must do 'more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it'' (Alice; Mayo). Claims that are nothing more than an instruction to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the abstract idea eligible (Alice). Examiners may, when appropriate, explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception. Consider overlap with other considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine/conventional) to assist analysis, but do not evaluate well-understood/routine/conventional in Step 2A Prong Two (that is for Step 2B). For formulating eligibility rejections see MPEP §2106.07(a). Key authorities: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank; Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus; Gottschalk v. Benson; BASCOM; McRO; Thales Visionix; Ultramercial; Electric Power Group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (result-oriented claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome — i.e., the claim fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished and instead attempts to cover any solution with no mechanism or steps described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result- or outcome-focused claims that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished are equivalent to 'apply it' and do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. In contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve the outcome may integrate the exception or provide significantly more. Examples/cases: Electric Power Group v. Alstom (caution against claims 'so result focused... as to effectively cover any solution'); Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (claims modifying an XML document lacked specifics and were ineligible). Other relevant cases: Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem. Use this consideration to determine whether claimed steps provide specific mechanisms or are merely functional results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking computers or other machinery merely as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as tools to perform an existing process (i.e., using devices in their ordinary capacity or appending a general-purpose computer to an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a computer or other machinery in its ordinary capacity (to receive, store, transmit data, etc.), or merely adding a general-purpose computer, does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Claims that merely invoke improved speed/efficiency from a general-purpose computer are insufficient. By contrast, claims that purport to improve computer capabilities or an existing technology may integrate the exception (see McRO, Enfish). Examples: Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (cellular telephone); TLI Communications v. AV Auto (server and telephone unit used in ordinary capacity); Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Capital One (tailoring information on a generic computer). See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for improvements to computer functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim's application of the judicial exception is particular (confined to a practical application) or general (broad applicability across many fields), which affects whether the claim provides meaningful limitations beyond the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims with broad applicability that generically recite an effect or claim every mode of accomplishing an effect may merely add the words 'apply it' and lack meaningful limitation (Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). Historical examples include O'Reilly v. Morse and The Telephone Cases. Conversely, limitations that confine the judicial exception to a particular, practical application may provide significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application — e.g., BASCOM (installation of a filtering tool at a specific location with customizable features confined abstract idea of filtering to a particular application) and DDR Holdings (technological solution to an Internet problem). Examiners should evaluate whether the limitation restricts the exception to a specific technological implementation or environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements add only insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception — activities incidental to the primary process or product that are nominal or tangential (pre-solution or post-solution activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra-solution activity includes pre-solution activities (e.g., gathering data) and post-solution activities (e.g., printing a report). The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity does not amount to an inventive concept, particularly when the activity is well-understood or conventional (Parker v. Flook; Mayo). Examiners should assess each claim on its merits and may consider other considerations (particular machine/transformation, field of use, well-understood/routine/conventional) to determine whether an element is insignificant extra-solution activity, but should not evaluate well-understood/routine/conventional in Step 2A Prong Two. Courts have identified categories of insignificant activity (enumerated below) and examiners should explain in rejections why such activities do not meaningfully limit the claim. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for rejection formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity: whether the limitation is well-known
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration (1) under 2106.05(g): whether the extra-solution limitation is well-known or conventional so that it is merely token or routine activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-known techniques or components used as extras (e.g., known random analysis techniques, known XML tags) have been treated as token extra-solution activity (Bilski v. Kappos; Flook; Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Erie Indem. Co.). Because this overlaps with the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration, it should not be considered in Step 2A Prong Two (reserved for Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity: whether the limitation is significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration (2) under 2106.05(g): whether the limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not merely nominal or tangential to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that are merely tangential or restrict access in ways that do not meaningfully limit the claimed invention have been found insignificant (Ultramercial v. Hulu; Apple v. Ameranth). This consideration is evaluated in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should assess whether the limitation meaningfully confines the claimed invention beyond the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity: whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering/outputting
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration (3) under 2106.05(g): whether the limitation is merely necessary data gathering or outputting that all uses of the recited judicial exception would require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities that merely gather input data or output results (presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining transaction information to verify credit cards, measuring biomarkers) have been treated as mere data gathering and insufficient to add significantly more (Mayo; OIP Technologies). This is considered in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examples of 'mere data gathering' and other illustrative categories (selecting data source/type, insignificant application such as cutting hair after determining style, printing/downloading generated menus) are provided in the guidance. Some cases also identify insignificant computer implementation as an example (Fort Properties; Bancorp Services), and MPEP §2106.05(f) discusses insignificant computer implementation further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use and Technological Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements amount to more than generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use; merely indicating a field of use or technological environment does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or adding token post-solution components does not make it patentable (Parker v. Flook; Bilski v. Kappos). Diamond v. Diehr explains that simply acquiescing to limiting the reach of a formula to a technological use is insufficient. The Flook example (mathematical formula used in a catalytic chemical conversion process) illustrates that tying a formula to a field of use does not add patentable subject matter. Examiners should not treat mere field-of-use limitations as providing significantly more than the judicial exception.
